fixes.explanation: The dream shows "…God’s angels were going up and down the ladder." (Gen 28:12) Notice it runs both ways, with the ladder resting on the earth and its top reaching up to heaven. Traffic in both directions, baker. That's what Jacob sees while he sleeps.

Not calm, baker. The text says Jacob was afraid, and then he says, “How awesome is this place!” (Gen 28:17) Just before that he says, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” (Gen 28:16) I bet finding out God was right there while I snoozed would shake me too.

Right, he's afraid. The text says Jacob was afraid, and he says, “How awesome is this place!” (Gen 28:17) Just before that he says, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” (Gen 28:16) That's the moment the fear shows up.

"Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…" (Gen 28:18) The stone he slept on is now standing up. Same stone, new job. Right after that, he calls the place Bethel (Gen 28:19).

Harvest never comes up in this passage. Esau says in his heart, "The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob." (Gen 27:41) The wait he names is the days of mourning for his father. I think this one hurts, baker.

No hunting party shows up in these verses. What Esau says in his heart is, "The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob." (Gen 27:41) That's the wait he names. I think this is a heavy moment, baker.

Rebekah tells Jacob, "…flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran." (Gen 27:43) She sends for him, warns him about Esau's plot, and has the destination ready right then. Laban is her own brother. I think this is a tense moment, baker, and she moves fast.
Deborah isn't in these verses at all. Rebekah tells Jacob, "…flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran." (Gen 27:43) The one she names is her own brother, Laban. And she says to go at once.

Eliezer isn't in this passage, baker. Plenty of names float around this family, so it's easy to grab the wrong one. Rebekah tells Jacob, "…flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran." (Gen 27:43) Laban is her brother, and that's who she names.

Hunger? Baker, a cookie fixes hunger. Rebekah says, "Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides…" (Gen 27:44) Fury is what she wants to see settle. She also says, "…until your brother’s rage against you wanes…" (Gen 27:45).

Egyptian isn't the word here. Rebekah says, "I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women." (Gen 27:46) Then she asks, "If Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them, what good is my life?" (Gen 27:46) The women she names are Hittite. The text doesn't say more about why, so I won't guess.

Philistine is a good guess, baker, but it's not in this verse. Rebekah says to Isaac, "I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women." (Gen 27:46) The word she picks is Hittite. She also asks what good her life is if Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them.

Isaac says, "And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants…" (Gen 28:4) He's asking God Almighty to give it, as the blessing in the verse before shows (Gen 28:3). Abraham is Isaac's own father (Gen 25:19). So the blessing is the one that goes back to his dad.

Noah isn't named in this blessing. Isaac says, "And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants…" (Gen 28:4) He's asking God Almighty for it (Gen 28:3). The name in the verse is Abraham, and he's Isaac's father (Gen 25:19).

Isaac asks that God give Jacob and his descendants the blessing of Abraham, "…so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham." (Gen 28:4) That's how the blessing ends. It's the land God gave to Abraham. And Isaac is asking God for it, not handing it out himself.

No branches here, baker. Jacob spent the night there "because the sun had set," and he took "…one of the stones from that place…" (Gen 28:11) The text says he put it under his head and lay down to sleep. A stone is what he picked.

A tower is a fair guess, since it also goes up high. But the dream isn't about one. The text says it was "…a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven…" (Gen 28:12) So Jacob sees a ladder, with its bottom on the earth and its top reaching heaven.

A mountain is a big picture, baker, but Jacob doesn't dream one. The verse says, "…a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven…" (Gen 28:12) What he sees is a ladder. Something to climb, with angels on it.

The LORD says, "I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie." (Gen 28:13) The land in the promise is the land under Jacob right then. He doesn't even have to get up to see the property, baker. And the promise is for his descendants too.

Carrying it to Haran isn't in the text. The verse says Jacob "…set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…" (Gen 28:18) That's what he does with the stone early that morning. The passage says nothing about him taking it along the road.

Jacob says, "…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…" (Gen 28:20) It's one more IF in his vow. The next verse says he wants to return safely to his father's house (Gen 28:21). Food, clothes and a safe road home, baker.

Servants and camels would be a big trip, baker, but they aren't in the vow. Jacob says, "…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…" (Gen 28:20) That's the IF he names. His next words are about returning safely to his father's house (Gen 28:21).
Jacob says, "…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth." (Gen 28:22) One out of every ten. I can count that on my mustache. Notice he says "all" that God gives him.

A third is a close guess, baker, but it's not the number in the verse. Jacob says, "…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth." (Gen 28:22) The word is tenth. He says it about all that God gives him.
